title: Monday Automations Alternatives: Best Options in 2026
summary: Monday automations alternatives include Zapier for non-technical teams, Make for visual builders, n8n for engineers, and Activepieces for self-hosting.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces for Cross-App and Self-Hosted Workflows


If your workflows start in monday.com but have to reach other apps, or you want an open-source tool you can run on your own servers, Activepieces fits. It's a poor choice for simple recipes that stay inside one board.


### Where Activepieces fits and where it doesn't


Start with what it won't do for you. **Activepieces doesn't make a board smarter** .


If your whole workflow is "when status changes to Done, notify the person column," monday's built-in automations already do that with no setup, and moving it elsewhere adds a second system to maintain for no gain.


Here is where[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/activepieces-credits-pricing-and-usage-2026-guide) earns its place, and it is the point this article keeps returning to: the work leaves the board.


A single flow can branch and call other apps, and a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, so there is no per-action quota to design around.


A missing connector is where a closed catalogue stalls, because it only grows on its vendor's schedule.


If the app you need isn't in Activepieces, AI can build the connector for you and it stays private to your own instance, so nothing waits on a release.


Its 750 integrations are counted from the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the MIT-licensed monorepo on GitHub, roughly 60% of them contributed by the community, and MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


Because the product is open source, a team that can't send data through a vendor's cloud can host it themselves. That's the trade the previous section described: you gain control and lose the convenience of someone else running the server.


Since the builder is also visual, a technically inclined ops person can maintain flows without writing code. Self-hosting, though, still needs someone who is comfortable deploying and updating it. If nobody on your team is, use the hosted version or another tool in this article.


### Worked workflow: a monday.com item change drives a cross-app update


Take a common cross-app case: a customer cancels a booked call, and several people need to know. The flow below uses Calendly, Slack and Gmail. The same shape works when the trigger is a monday.com item change instead, with the later steps unchanged.


In the screenshot, a three-step flow sits in the Activepieces builder. The trigger is Calendly's "Event Canceled," followed by "Send Message To A Channel" in Slack and "Send Email" in Gmail.


The right panel shows the trigger configured with a personal token and the scope set to User, and the sample data returns an "invitee.canceled" event marked "Tested Successfully."


What to take from it: the trigger was tested against a real event payload before anything downstream was built. Because of that, you see the actual fields you can map into the Slack message and the email.


That test step is the habit worth copying. Run the trigger, read the sample data, and only then wire up the actions. Once it passes, each later step can draw on the fields you just saw, rather than on guesses about what the app sends.


### Check connector coverage before you commit


Before committing, check that the apps your workflow touches are covered. The full list of connectors, which Activepieces calls pieces, is at[https://www.activepieces.com/integrations](https://www.activepieces.com/integrations) .


You can start free and build a flow like the one above to see whether the builder suits the person who will own it.
